answer.evidence: The main body is topped by a large sloped tiled roof (rows 4-61). At x=72 it runs rows 4-42 and ends at a light eave edge line. The cream clapboard gable wall below it, with windows, balcony and door, forms a front face of about 93 rows (rows 43-135). The lower-left balcony roof (rows 89-103) is a second tiled slope, so both major roof parts show a top surface. The right slope is a darker roof plane, not an isometric side wall.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a clean, modern-looking house. Its outlines are tinted (dark blue-grey beside the roof, dark olive beside the siding), and only 2% of dark edge pixels are neutral, so they are not near-black. Flat-fill coverage is 2%, close to the references' 0%. The measured numbers do not mark it as shallow, but it falls short by eye. The blue-grey roof has about 4 tones with faint tile rows and no per-tile highlights or scallops. The cream siding has about 3 tones and relies on regular horizontal lines instead of speckle or grain. The balcony, door and windows are simple, with few tones. Visible tones per tile are 9, against 12 and 10 for the references, so it is lower on the primary density fact. Next to the references (roof tiles lit one by one, plaster speckle, stones shaded individually) it reads as smoother and flatter, closer to vector art. It is not a plain sticker, but I would not accept it as equal to the references.

answer.evidence: The main body is a two-storey house seen from the south. The silhouette widens row by row from 3 px at row 4 to 122 px at row 24, and the tile-textured roof planes (left light, right dark) meet at a central ridge. The roof runs from row 4 to about row 61 and ends in a lighter eave edge, so it counts as roof-plane evidence (c). Below it is a tall front face (cream siding gable wall, windows, balcony, entrance door, ground-floor sliding window) from about row 62 to row 135. The lower shed roof at rows 89-98 also shows tile rows ending in an edge line at rows 102-103. The balcony railing is a front-facing vertical face on a thin slab, which is a minor part. The drawing is a clear top surface plus a front face of 3+ rows, so it reads as three_quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is the right kind (a whole building) and the outlines are tinted: only 2% of dark edge pixels are neutral, and the roof edge leans dark blue-grey with dark olive beside the siding. So it is not a sticker outline. Near-flat coverage is 2% against 0% for both references, so there are no big flat fills. Siding lines, window grids, the balcony rail and the door add some texture. It still falls short of the references. The slate roof has only about 4 steps, in broad panels with faint horizontal tile lines and no per-tile highlights. The yellow walls are about 3-4 steps (base, line, shadow) with no plaster speckle or grain. The references have scalloped tiles with highlights, and shaded stones or timber. Visible tones per tile are 9, against 12 and 10 for the references. Raw colours per tile are 9 against 18 and 11, and total colours are 45 against 185 and 66. Overall it reads as cleaner, flatter and more vector-like than the Beodeul pieces. With the shading steps and texture both below the bar, and the rule to fail when in doubt, it fails.
